notes.text: Cannot I do — That God hath an absolute sovereign power to do what he pleases with the work of his hands: but he acts as a just judge, rendering to every man according to his works.

glossa.text: *The word that came to Jeremias from the Lord, saying. ((HIER.))* Through all the senses unto judgment, etc., *as far as* and there to hear the precepts of the Lord.
*And it was marred,* etc. Marred by divine providence, that the craftsman, unknowing, might by his own mistake figure forth the parable.
*Suddenly I will speak. ((ID.))* Free choice it signifies, etc., *as far as* that in all things the grace of the giver may excel.
*Behold I frame evil against you. ((HIER.))* He fulfils the parable which he taught both by sight and by speech.

notes.text: Afar off — Thou knowest what my thoughts will be in such and such circumstances, long before I know it, yea from all eternity.
Compassest — Thou discernest every step I take. It is a metaphor from soldiers besieging their enemies, and setting watches round about them.
Beset me — With thy all-seeing providence. And laid - Thou keepest me, as it were with a strong hand, in thy sight and under thy power.
I cannot — Apprehend in what manner thou dost so presently know all things.

glossa.text: *Unto the end, a psalm of David* *Ddvid**.* ((CASS.)) A psalm full of the depth of mysteries, etc., *as far as* veiled in the prophets, manifest in the Gospel. ((AUG.)) The whole Christ speaks, as one entire man, etc., *as far as* as two in one flesh. *Lord, thou hast proved me.* ((CASS.)) First, concerning the knowledge of God, etc., *as far as* fourthly, how the wicked do him no hurt, there, *If thou wilt kill, O God,* etc. *Lord, thou hast proved.* ((AUG.)) Now restored in Jerusalem, etc., *as far as* this is the person of the whole of human nature returning.

*Thou hast understood.* ((CASS.)) The foreknowledge of the Godhead is here shown, etc., *as far as* because the manhood assumed cannot be made equal to the divine substance. *From afar off.* ((AUG.)) While I am still on pilgrimage, before I come to the fatherland, as the father ran to meet the younger son returning, because he understood his thoughts from afar off, because he had said within himself, worn out with want *egestare*: *I will arise and go to my father.*

*My path,* namely the evil one, by which I went, forsaking my father.

*And the line.* (Otherwise) the boundary, how far I came: far indeed had I gone, but thou wast there. He speaks as a fugitive caught, the vengeance of God following after him.

*And all my ways:* before I went in them; and thou didst permit me to go in labour, that I might return if I would not labour: this I confess. *For there is no guile in my tongue:* now I have justified in thy grace.

My *last things,* when I fed the swine, *The old things,* when I asked for the portion of the substance: this according to the parable. But mystically, *The old things,* when through the ancient sin *pecatum* we fell: *The last things,* the penalty, when we came into this mortality, which is the last, if we are willing to return; otherwise the eternal remains. *Thou hast formed me,* unto labours, unto which we are all born. *Thou hast laid.* (Otherwise) Thou hast made heavy the hand, the avenging hand, weighing down the proud man wholesomely, that it may raise up the humble man, in the hand made heavy.

*Wonderful,* and incomprehensible *incomprehensibllis* to me. *Thy knowledge is become.* It is not easy for me to contemplate thee, whom in my pride I forsook, as it was before, when I was with thee, when I said, give me the portion of the substance. *From me,* that is, from my sin.

*It is strengthened,* (otherwise) it has prevailed. *And I shall not be able* to attain to it of myself. ((AUG.)) In Exodus it is read that the Lord, etc., *as far as* I am not hidden from thee, whose boundary thou seest.

notes.text: This single epistle infinitely transcends all the wisdom of the world. And it gives us a specimen how Christians ought to treat of secular affairs from higher principles. Paul a prisoner of Christ — To whom, as such, Philemon could deny nothing. And Timotheus - This was written before the second epistle to Timothy, ver. xxii.
To Apphia — His wife, to whom also the business in part belonged. And the church in thy house - The Christians who meet there.
Hearing — Probably from Onesimus.
I pray that the communication of thy faith may become effectual — That is, that thy faith may be effectually communicated to others, who see and acknowledge thy piety and charity.
The saints — To whom Philemon's house was open, verse ii.
I might be bold in Christ — Through the authority he hath given me.

Yet out of love I rather entreat thee — In how handsome a manner does the apostle just hint, and immediately drop, the consideration of his power to command, and tenderly entreat Philemon to hearken to his friend, his aged friend, and now prisoner for Christ! With what endearment, in the next verse, does he call Onesimus his son, before he names his name! And as soon as he had mentioned it, with what fine address does he just touch on his former faults, and instantly pass on to the happy change that was now made upon him! So disposing Philemon to attend to his request, and the motives wherewith he was going to enforce it.
Whom I have begotten in my bonds — The son of my age.
Now profitable — None should be expected to be a good servant before he is a good man. He manifestly alludes to his name, Onesimus, which signifies profitable.
Receive him, that is, my own bowels — Whom I love as my own soul. Such is the natural affection of a father in Christ toward his spiritual children.
To serve me in thy stead — To do those services for me which thou, if present, wouldest gladly have done thyself.
That thy benefit might not be by constraint — For Philemon could not have refused it.
God might permit him to be separated (a soft word) for a season, that thou mightest have him forever — Both on earth and in heaven.
In the flesh — As a dutiful servant. In the Lord - As a fellow- Christian.
If thou accountest me a partner — So that thy things are mine, and mine are thine.

I will repay it — If thou requirest it. Not to say, that then owest me thyself - It cannot be expressed, how great our obligation is to those who have gained our souls to Christ. Beside - Receiving Onesimus.
Refresh my bowels in Christ — Give me the most exquisite and Christian pleasure.

glossa.text: *Paul a prisoner.* He does not say, *An apostle:* which is a name of dignity, but *a prisoner,* which is a name of humility: because he does not command, but entreats. For here there is an intercession on behalf of Onesimus: therefore he calls to mind the things which belong to humility, beginning from his own injury, so that he might give dignity to his own Epistle. For as to be bound by reason of sin is a reproach, so on the contrary to endure the bonds of custody for Christ is the greatest glory. At that time, therefore, he was in custody. Therefore he says that he is a prisoner.
*Which thou hast.* For because he believed in Christ and loved him; he believed the saints and loved them, and thus through the works of faith and charity he served Christ and the saints.

*That the communication.* As if he should say: Thou hast faith and charity in Christ and in the saints, so that *the communication of thy faith may be made evident,* that is, that thy faith be communicating with our faith; or, that what thou communicatest to others out of thy faith may be evident. And this, *In the acknowledgment of all.* That is, let it be so evident, let all good hereby be deservedly known to be in thee through Christ, that is, the sufficiency of all good things. As thus: I am mindful of thee, and I give thanks in the prayers held concerning this, that *the communication of thy faith,* that is, the working of faith by which thou servest Christ and the saints, *may be made evident in the acknowledgment which is. In Christ Jesus.* That is, with the knowledge of the eternal good, that it may be looked for as a reward. For this the Apostle prays, that that man's working may be done with the knowledge of goodness, that is, that he may work with such a mind that from it he may look for Jesus Christ as a reward in the time to come, and not the recompense of temporal things.

*The bowels of the saints.* That is, the most beloved sons of the saints, or, the affection of the saints, inclined toward thee, has rested in thee, thee namely consoling, and has been refreshed, because they have found thee good in all things.

*I beseech thee.* It is a great thing, not in the case of a lowly man, but of an exalted one, if he bows himself and beseeches. *An old man.* One ought the more to comply with an old man, by the likeness of age.

*Who was once to thee,* etc. ((CHRYS.)) See how prudently he confesses the fault of that very man, namely of Onesimus, that by that very thing he may extinguish the master's anger; he does not say: Now he will be useful to thee, lest that man should not believe it, but he brought in his own person as well, that from this that man might be able the more worthily to hope for better things. For if he is going to be useful to Paul, who exacts so great a diligence of virtue and of perfection, how much more to his master.

*As my own bowels,* etc. The Apostle, while he was in custody, baptized Onesimus, a fugitive running back to the divine help, seeing in him the hope of usefulness: whom he so commends that he signifies that his own soul is received in him.
*For perhaps.* He therefore says *perhaps,* because human things are doubtful, and there could have been another cause why God so disposed it.

*Most of all to me.* To me, thy teacher: the brother Onesimus, his own master having been offended, fled for refuge to the Apostle to this end, that, his sins being blotted out, he might return useful, so far that he might be made not only equal in merits to his own master, but a brother to the teacher himself. And lest Philemon (because he is master) should be puffed up against the slave, he humbles him, saying: *A brother also in the flesh,* because all are from one Adam, and *in the Lord* through faith.

*Impute this to me.* Now he tears away every excuse, when he says that it must be imputed to himself, if he has either done harm or owes anything.

*So brother may I enjoy thee in the Lord.* That is, I shall rejoice over thee in the kingdom of God, if thou shalt do what I ask. And what that is, he subjoins: *Refresh the bowels,* etc.

*Trusting in obedience.* He provokes him by coaxing him thus, so that he may not do more than is asked of him *non amplius*; read *amplius*, "that he may do more than is asked". For it is wont to happen that he who sees himself well thought of shows himself the better.

notes.text: If any man come to me, and hate not his father — Comparatively to Christ: yea, so as actually to renounce his field, oxen, wife, all things, and act as if he hated them, when they stand in competition with him. Matt. x, 37.
And which of you intending to build a tower — That is, and whoever of you intends to follow me, let him first seriously weigh these things.
Another king — Does this mean, the prince of this world? Certainly he has greater numbers on his side. How numerous are his children and servants!

glossa.text: *And there went crowds,* etc. The crowds that follow Jesus as he makes his way to Jerusalem signify those who, invited or compelled, come to the supper, and with their whole intent imitate Jesus going before them to the vision of eternal peace. These therefore he instructs, who ought with sincere love to seek that country, and for its sake to renounce the affections of carnal love.

*If any man come.* We can at once both hate and love: so that we love both those joined to us by acquaintance and by the divine precept, and those whom we suffer as adversaries in the way of God we may not know, by hating and fleeing them. *Yea more.* Then do we rightly hate our own soul, when we do not consent to its carnal desires, but struggle against them and break them.

*And whosoever doth not carry.* The cross is carried in two ways: either when the flesh is afflicted by abstinence, or when the mind is afflicted by compassion for a neighbour. *And come after me.* For if a man tears his flesh for empty glory, or has compassion on his neighbour carnally so as to favour his fault, he seems to bear the cross, but he does not follow God.

*For which of you.* After the Lord had given to those following him into Jerusalem lofty precepts concerning contempt of the world and the casting away of the body, he adds a precept concerning perseverance, for which patience with humility is necessary. And this by the likeness of one that builds. *To build a tower.* Because he had given lofty precepts, he subjoins a comparison of a loftiness to be built. *Reckoneth the charges.* He reckons the charges who discerns that temporal money must be paid out, and the heart turned away from the covetous desires of the world, and the soul made ready against the adversities of the world.

*All that see.* As the Apostle says: *We are made a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men ((II Cor. IV))*. And in everything that we do we ought to consider our hidden adversaries, who lie in wait for our works; and unless we watch against them, we suffer as mockers those whom we have as persuaders to evil.

*Or what,* etc. After the similitude of the tower to be built, he adds the similitude of a greater matter, of a king about to fight. In which it is shown that by the fulfilment of the preceding commandments no man can attain to glory unless the sentence of the severe judge be tempered by mercy. For in the sight of God every man is imperfect. *If he be able.* He meets God as it were with ten thousand who offers the works of the ten commandments which he has performed outwardly. But God comes against him as it were with a doubled number, when he examines him, scarcely prepared in work alone, at once concerning both work and thought. And therefore, while he is still far off through the delay of the judgment, we, considering the insufficiency of our frailty, ought to send before us, for the obtaining of the severe judge's peace, an embassy of tears, of good works, of holy affection.

*So likewise,* etc. He infers this from the foregoing similitudes. Since he cannot build well who does not reckon the charges, nor can he safely go to meet another who does not send an embassy before him, therefore neither can he be my disciple who does not renounce all things.

echoes.text: As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to those who send him; for he refreshes the soul of his masters.
echoes.note: Paul says the hearts (literally bowels/inward parts) of the saints have been 'refreshed' through Philemon. Proverbs likens a faithful messenger to the cold of snow that 'refreshes the soul' of his masters, the nearest sapiential parallel to this language of inward refreshment. The link is verbal and thematic rather than a citation, and Paul develops it more pointedly at v20.

echoes.text: “‘If your brother has grown poor among you, and sells himself to you; you shall not make him to serve as a slave. As a hired servant, and as a temporary resident, he shall be with you; he shall serve with you until the Year of Jubilee: then he shall go out from you, he and his children with him, and shall return to his own family, and to the possession of his fathers. For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. They shall not be […]
echoes.note: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus 'no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother.' The Holiness Code forbids treating an impoverished Israelite who sells himself as a slave, requiring instead that he be held as a hired worker and a brother, not ruled over harshly. Paul effectively extends this Israelite kinship-over-bondage principle to a Christian master and his returning slave.

echoes.text: If your brother, a Hebrew man, or a Hebrew woman, is sold to you, and serves you six years; then in the seventh year you shall let him go free from you. When you let him go free from you, you shall not let him go empty. You shall furnish him liberally out of your flock, out of your threshing floor, and out of your wine press. As Yahweh your God has blessed you, you shall give to him. You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and […]
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic slave law mandates release of a Hebrew bondservant and generous provision out of remembered solidarity ('you were a slave in Egypt'). Paul's reconfiguring of Onesimus from slave to beloved brother, no longer held under necessity, resonates with this manumission-and-fraternity ethic, though Paul never cites the statute.

echoes.text: You shall not deliver to his master a servant who has escaped from his master to you. He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place which he shall choose within one of your gates, where it pleases him best. You shall not oppress him.
echoes.note: The law forbids returning an escaped slave to his master and requires letting him dwell freely where he chooses. Paul's careful handling of the fugitive Onesimus, sending him back only as a free brother and asking Philemon not to reclaim him as property, stands in deliberate tension and dialogue with this provision. Many read the whole letter as Paul navigating around the spirit of this command.

echoes.text: Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life. For these two years the famine has been in the land, and there are yet five years, in which there will be neither plowing nor harvest. God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant in the earth, and to save you alive by a great deliverance. So now it wasn’t you who sent me here, but God, and he has made me a father to Pharaoh, lord […]
echoes.note: 'Perhaps he was separated from you for a while, that you would have him forever' echoes Joseph's providential reading of his own separation from his family: 'God sent me before you to preserve life... it was not you who sent me here, but God.' Paul, like Joseph, reframes a painful parting as hidden divine purpose that yields a greater, lasting reunion.

echoes.text: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save many people alive.
echoes.note: Joseph's summary, 'you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good,' undergirds Paul's 'perhaps' of v15, where Onesimus's wrong and flight are recast as occasion for good. The thematic kinship is strong even though Paul borrows no wording.

echoes.text: Laban said to him, “Surely you are my bone and my flesh.” He lived with him for a month.
echoes.note: Onesimus is now to be received as a brother 'both in the flesh and in the Lord.' Laban's welcome of Jacob, 'surely you are my bone and my flesh,' is the paradigmatic Hebrew idiom for kinship recognition that overrides prior status. The connection is faint and conceptual.

echoes.text: I’ll be collateral for him. From my hand will you require him. If I don’t bring him to you, and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever,
echoes.note: 'If he has wronged you or owes you anything, put that to my account... I will repay it' enacts the role of surety. Judah pledges himself for Benjamin: 'I will be surety for him; of my hand you shall require him.' Paul stands as personal guarantor for Onesimus exactly as Judah does for his brother, assuming the debt against himself.

echoes.text: For your servant became collateral for the boy to my father, saying, ‘If I don’t bring him to you, then I will bear the blame to my father forever.’
echoes.note: Judah restates his suretyship before Joseph, 'I became surety for the boy to my father,' offering to bear the consequence in the brother's place. Paul's handwritten pledge to absorb Onesimus's debt and stand in his stead closely parallels this self-substituting guarantee for a kinsman.

echoes.text: My son, if you have become collateral for your neighbor, if you have struck your hands in pledge for a stranger; You are trapped by the words of your mouth. You are ensnared with the words of your mouth. Do this now, my son, and deliver yourself, since you have come into the hand of your neighbor. Go, humble yourself. Press your plea with your neighbor.
echoes.note: Proverbs repeatedly treats the giving of surety for another as a weighty, self-binding act ('if you have struck your hands in pledge for a stranger... you are snared by the words of your mouth'). Paul knowingly takes on precisely this binding pledge for Onesimus, inverting the proverb's caution into voluntary love.

echoes.text: He who is collateral for a stranger will suffer for it, but he who refuses pledges of collateral is secure.
echoes.note: 'He who is surety for a stranger will suffer for it.' Paul's assumption of Onesimus's liability deliberately embraces the cost the proverb warns against, making the sapiential surety-language a backdrop for his act of intercession.

echoes.text: As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to those who send him; for he refreshes the soul of his masters.
echoes.note: 'Refresh my heart in the Lord' picks up the language of inward refreshment from v7. Proverbs' image of the faithful messenger who 'refreshes the soul of his masters' is the closest wisdom parallel to this petition for refreshment as the fruit of obedient love.

echoes.text: It fell on a day, that Elisha passed to Shunem, where there was a prominent woman; and she persuaded him to eat bread. So it was, that as often as he passed by, he turned in there to eat bread. She said to her husband, “See now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God, that passes by us continually. Please let us make a little room on the wall. Let us set for him there a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp stand. It shall be, when he comes to us, that he […]
echoes.note: 'Prepare a guest room for me' faintly recalls the Shunammite woman who prepares a small upper room for Elisha so the man of God may lodge with her. The shared motif is hospitality of a lodging readied for an honored servant of God, though Paul uses ordinary travel language without scriptural signal.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.
echoes.note: 'If anyone... doesn't disregard his own father, mother, wife, children' echoes the blessing of Levi, who said of father and mother 'I have not seen him,' disowned his brothers and ignored his children — keeping covenant fidelity above kin. The radical preference of covenant loyalty over family ties is the closest scriptural precedent for Jesus' hyperbolic 'hate.'

echoes.text: He said to them, “Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, ‘Every man put his sword on his thigh, and go back and forth from gate to gate throughout the camp, and every man kill his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbor.’” The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses: and there fell of the people that day about three thousand men. Moses said, “Consecrate yourselves today to Yahweh, yes, every man against his son, and against […]
echoes.note: The Levites' ordination by slaying brother, companion, and neighbor at Moses' command — 'each one at the cost of his son and his brother' — is the narrative behind Deut 33:9's praise of Levi. It models the disciple's willingness to set covenant allegiance above family, coherent with Jesus' demand and the cross-bearing that follows.

echoes.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
echoes.note: Micah's portrait of eschatological family division — son dishonoring father, daughter against mother, 'a man's enemies are the men of his own household' — undergirds Jesus' setting discipleship against the closest kin (and is explicitly cited at Luke 12:53). Recurrence in Luke strengthens its availability here.

echoes.text: If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son, or your daughter, or the wife of your bosom, or your friend, who is as your own soul, entices you secretly, saying, “Let us go and serve other gods,” which you have not known, you, nor your fathers; of the gods of the peoples who are around you, near to you, or far off from you, from the one end of the earth even to the other end of the earth; you shall not consent to him, nor listen to him; neither […]
echoes.note: The command to show no pity even to a brother, son, daughter, or wife who entices to false worship — placing exclusive devotion to the Lord above the dearest relations — offers a Torah analogue to subordinating family to higher allegiance. Faint and contested, but coheres with the covenant-over-kin theme of Deut 33:9.

echoes.text: for by wise guidance you wage your war; and victory is in many advisors.
echoes.note: The king who 'will not sit down first and consider' before going to war reflects the proverb 'by wise guidance you can wage your war, and in an abundance of counselors there is victory.' The counsel to deliberate before battle is the sapiential ground of Jesus' second illustration about counting the cost.

echoes.text: Plans are established by advice; by wise guidance you wage war!
echoes.note: 'Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war' doubles the counting-the-cost-before-war motif of vv.31-32. Recurrence of this maxim across Proverbs 20:18 and 24:6 strengthens the wisdom-deliberation background of the tower-and-war pair.

echoes.text: Prepare your work outside, and get your fields ready. Afterwards, build your house.
echoes.note: 'Prepare your work outside... and after that build your house' supplies the prudence-before-building logic behind the tower illustration ('count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it'). Faint but coherent with the sapiential planning theme.

echoes.text: Let reason be the beginning of every work, And let counsel go before every action.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's 'before every action let counsel go, and before every undertaking deliberation' captures the count-the-cost-first principle of both illustrations. Deuterocanonical availability adds Second-Temple recurrence to the wisdom-deliberation reading.

notes.text: Chuse life — They shall have life that chuse it: they that chuse the favour of God, and communion with him, shall have what they chuse. They that come short of life and happiness, must thank themselves only. They had had them, if they had chosen them, when they were put to their choice: but they die, because they will die.

That thou mayest love the Lord thy God — Here he shews them in short, what their duty is; To love God as the Lord, a being most amiable, and as their God, a God in covenant with them: as an evidence of their love, to obey his voice in every thing, and by constancy in this love and obedience, to cleave to him all their days. And what encouragement had they to do this? For he is thy life and the length of thy days - He gives life, preserves life, restores life, and prolongs it, by his power, tho' it be a frail life, and by his presence, tho' it be a forfeited life. He sweetens life by his comforts, and compleats all in life everlasting. Moses encourages the people and Joshua, ver. 1-8. 23. Delivers to the priests the law, to be read every seventh year, ver. 9-13. God informs Moses of his approaching death, and the future apostasy of Israel, ver. 14-18. Orders him to write a song, which should be a testimony against them, ver. 19-22. Moses gives the law to the Levites to lay up beside the ark, and bids them assemble the people to hear his song, ver. 24-30.

Blessed — The Hebrew words are very emphatical: O the blessedness of that man! Counsel - That doth not lead his life according to their counsel, or manner of living. Standeth - Which notes a more settled abode in it. Way - In their manner of conversation. Seat - Which notes a constant and resolved perseverance in their wicked courses. Scornful - Of those who make a mock of sin, and scoff at goodness and goodmen. Divers observe a gradation in this verse; the following clause still exceeding the former, for standing is more than walking, and sitting more than standing; and sinners in scripture use, are worse than the ungodly, and the scornful are the worst of sinners.
Day and night — Not seldom and slightly, but diligently, and constantly.
Whither — His happiness is not short and transitory, but, like those trees which are continually green and flourishing.
Ungodly — Their condition is far different. Chaff - They are restless and unquiet: their seeming felicity, hath no firm foundation, but quickly vanishes and flees away as chaff before the wind.
Not stand — Not endure the trial. Judgment - In the great and general judgment of the world.

Knoweth — He approves, loves, and delights in them, and therefore will recompence them. Perish - All their designs and courses shall come to nothing, and they shall perish with them. There is nothing in this psalm which is not applicable to Christ, but some things which are not all applicable to David. Threatenings denounced against the adversaries of Christ's kingdom, ver. 1-6. Promises made to Christ, ver. 7-9. Counsel given to all, to submit to him, ver. 10-12.

glossa.text: « Blessed is the man who hath not gone away, etc. » ((AUG., Enarr. in Psal., tom. III.)) The order, Adam went away when he withdrew from God; he stood, when he was delighted with sin; he sat, when, confirmed in pride, he could not return, save as set free by this man, who had none of these things. Adam went away when he consented to the persuasion of the devil; he stood, while he ate the apple; he sat, while he excused himself: « The woman whom thou gavest me seduced me. » ((Gen. III)) . After the likeness of exiles, who, while they are on the road, are more easily called back, while they now stand, with more difficulty: at length with the greatest difficulty, when they have there been made masters and lords. ((REMI.)) There is sinning by thought, by act, and by words in teaching. ((CASS.)) The impious man is so against God, the sinner against himself, the pestilent man against his neighbour. « In the chair, giving an example of sinning. » ((CASS.)) The throne is of kings, the tribunal of judges, the chair properly of teachers. ((Ibid.)) It is as though he said: You who have fallen through the first Adam, be ye conformed to this second one: because the blessed man is the contrary of the first

« But in the law. » AUG. ((CASS.)) Here he is shown full of every good in himself. ((AUG.)) It is not perfect praise to flee the things to be blamed, unless the things to be praised follow. In the order in which they grew in the first man, they are taken away in the second.

« In the law. » ((Ibid.)) He who is in the law acts according to the law, he who is under the law is acted upon according to the law: the one is free, the other a slave. ((Ibid. AMBR.)) One thing is the law which is written for him that serves, another that which is beheld with the mind by him who has no need of letters. « The will. » ((CASS.)) That there be no weariness of labour, nor idleness, but he shall meditate always. The will of sense is under the law; of reason, in the law; of divinity, above the law.

« And he shall be. » ((Ibid.)) Here he is shown useful to us, giving the fruit of life, and leaves, and overshadowing us, « Blessed is the man. But in the law. And he shall be. » The full definition of the blessed man. All these things belong not to every blessed man, but to Christ alone. « As a tree. » ((Ibid.)) After the likeness of the tree of life which is in paradise, whereof obedient man was to have eaten. « A tree. » ((Ibid.)) In paradise there is the tree of life, a tree unto life, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. « Of waters. » ((AUG.)) The waters are the Holy Spirit, according to that word: « He that shall have believed in me, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water ((Joan. VII)), » and it is against the heats of the vices. ((CASS.)) Or, by water, the wisdom of God, by which the inner man is restored, as thirst by water. ((AUG.)) Or the mortal race, as Job: « Many waters, many peoples, » because they flow down into death, as waters into the sea. « He shall give. » ((Ibid.)) To give pertains to the rational sense and to the will of the one offering. « And the leaf. » ((Ibid.)) As the leaves cover the fruit, so the words of the Lord guard his promises. « And all things. » ((Ibid.)) Why go through them one by one.

« Not so the impious. » Here by the vengeance upon the wicked he terrifies the adverse, the dread of these makes what has gone before more welcome. « From the face of the earth. » ((AUG.)) Of eternal stability, because as this earth nourishes and holds up a man, so that other earth holds up the inner man.

« Therefore they shall not rise again. » Because the wind casteth them away, that is, therefore, because they have been given over to a reprobate sense: therefore they do not rise again in the first resurrection, that they may judge themselves in counsel, that they may set the wills of God before their own. Or in the council, that is, in the harmonious multitude of the just, the impious idolaters, or apostates. Sinners, false Christians: or else therefore they do not rise again in the time to come, that they may judge, or that, being judged, they may rest in the council, that is, in the college of the just. « In judgment, etc. » In the judgment there will be four orders: some shall judge and shall not be judged, as the most perfect; some shall neither judge nor be judged, as the damned unbelievers; some shall be judged and shall be saved, as the moderately good; some shall be judged and shall perish, as the evil faithful. « In the council. » ((AUG.)) In the eternal good, to follow which was counsel to the saints. « Or in the council, » in the judgment, that they may judge together with them; for there is judgment when different sins are punished with different penalties; and it is said from this by likeness. « They rise again. » What resurrections these are: of the soul, from sins in the present; of the body, from death in the time to come, whereby it shall be made impassible and immortal.
« For the Lord knoweth, etc., » That is, these do not rise again in the soul, because God does not approve their works, but those of the just only.

notes.text: This single epistle infinitely transcends all the wisdom of the world. And it gives us a specimen how Christians ought to treat of secular affairs from higher principles. Paul a prisoner of Christ — To whom, as such, Philemon could deny nothing. And Timotheus - This was written before the second epistle to Timothy, ver. xxii.
To Apphia — His wife, to whom also the business in part belonged. And the church in thy house - The Christians who meet there.
Hearing — Probably from Onesimus.
I pray that the communication of thy faith may become effectual — That is, that thy faith may be effectually communicated to others, who see and acknowledge thy piety and charity.
The saints — To whom Philemon's house was open, verse ii.
I might be bold in Christ — Through the authority he hath given me.

Yet out of love I rather entreat thee — In how handsome a manner does the apostle just hint, and immediately drop, the consideration of his power to command, and tenderly entreat Philemon to hearken to his friend, his aged friend, and now prisoner for Christ! With what endearment, in the next verse, does he call Onesimus his son, before he names his name! And as soon as he had mentioned it, with what fine address does he just touch on his former faults, and instantly pass on to the happy change that was now made upon him! So disposing Philemon to attend to his request, and the motives wherewith he was going to enforce it.
Whom I have begotten in my bonds — The son of my age.
Now profitable — None should be expected to be a good servant before he is a good man. He manifestly alludes to his name, Onesimus, which signifies profitable.
Receive him, that is, my own bowels — Whom I love as my own soul. Such is the natural affection of a father in Christ toward his spiritual children.
To serve me in thy stead — To do those services for me which thou, if present, wouldest gladly have done thyself.
That thy benefit might not be by constraint — For Philemon could not have refused it.
God might permit him to be separated (a soft word) for a season, that thou mightest have him forever — Both on earth and in heaven.
In the flesh — As a dutiful servant. In the Lord - As a fellow- Christian.
If thou accountest me a partner — So that thy things are mine, and mine are thine.

I will repay it — If thou requirest it. Not to say, that then owest me thyself - It cannot be expressed, how great our obligation is to those who have gained our souls to Christ. Beside - Receiving Onesimus.
Refresh my bowels in Christ — Give me the most exquisite and Christian pleasure.

glossa.text: *Paul a prisoner.* He does not say, *An apostle:* which is a name of dignity, but *a prisoner,* which is a name of humility: because he does not command, but entreats. For here there is an intercession on behalf of Onesimus: therefore he calls to mind the things which belong to humility, beginning from his own injury, so that he might give dignity to his own Epistle. For as to be bound by reason of sin is a reproach, so on the contrary to endure the bonds of custody for Christ is the greatest glory. At that time, therefore, he was in custody. Therefore he says that he is a prisoner.
*Which thou hast.* For because he believed in Christ and loved him; he believed the saints and loved them, and thus through the works of faith and charity he served Christ and the saints.

*That the communication.* As if he should say: Thou hast faith and charity in Christ and in the saints, so that *the communication of thy faith may be made evident,* that is, that thy faith be communicating with our faith; or, that what thou communicatest to others out of thy faith may be evident. And this, *In the acknowledgment of all.* That is, let it be so evident, let all good hereby be deservedly known to be in thee through Christ, that is, the sufficiency of all good things. As thus: I am mindful of thee, and I give thanks in the prayers held concerning this, that *the communication of thy faith,* that is, the working of faith by which thou servest Christ and the saints, *may be made evident in the acknowledgment which is. In Christ Jesus.* That is, with the knowledge of the eternal good, that it may be looked for as a reward. For this the Apostle prays, that that man's working may be done with the knowledge of goodness, that is, that he may work with such a mind that from it he may look for Jesus Christ as a reward in the time to come, and not the recompense of temporal things.

*The bowels of the saints.* That is, the most beloved sons of the saints, or, the affection of the saints, inclined toward thee, has rested in thee, thee namely consoling, and has been refreshed, because they have found thee good in all things.

*I beseech thee.* It is a great thing, not in the case of a lowly man, but of an exalted one, if he bows himself and beseeches. *An old man.* One ought the more to comply with an old man, by the likeness of age.

*Who was once to thee,* etc. ((CHRYS.)) See how prudently he confesses the fault of that very man, namely of Onesimus, that by that very thing he may extinguish the master's anger; he does not say: Now he will be useful to thee, lest that man should not believe it, but he brought in his own person as well, that from this that man might be able the more worthily to hope for better things. For if he is going to be useful to Paul, who exacts so great a diligence of virtue and of perfection, how much more to his master.

*As my own bowels,* etc. The Apostle, while he was in custody, baptized Onesimus, a fugitive running back to the divine help, seeing in him the hope of usefulness: whom he so commends that he signifies that his own soul is received in him.
*For perhaps.* He therefore says *perhaps,* because human things are doubtful, and there could have been another cause why God so disposed it.

*Most of all to me.* To me, thy teacher: the brother Onesimus, his own master having been offended, fled for refuge to the Apostle to this end, that, his sins being blotted out, he might return useful, so far that he might be made not only equal in merits to his own master, but a brother to the teacher himself. And lest Philemon (because he is master) should be puffed up against the slave, he humbles him, saying: *A brother also in the flesh,* because all are from one Adam, and *in the Lord* through faith.

*Impute this to me.* Now he tears away every excuse, when he says that it must be imputed to himself, if he has either done harm or owes anything.

*So brother may I enjoy thee in the Lord.* That is, I shall rejoice over thee in the kingdom of God, if thou shalt do what I ask. And what that is, he subjoins: *Refresh the bowels,* etc.

*Trusting in obedience.* He provokes him by coaxing him thus, so that he may not do more than is asked of him *non amplius*; read *amplius*, "that he may do more than is asked". For it is wont to happen that he who sees himself well thought of shows himself the better.

notes.text: If any man come to me, and hate not his father — Comparatively to Christ: yea, so as actually to renounce his field, oxen, wife, all things, and act as if he hated them, when they stand in competition with him. Matt. x, 37.
And which of you intending to build a tower — That is, and whoever of you intends to follow me, let him first seriously weigh these things.
Another king — Does this mean, the prince of this world? Certainly he has greater numbers on his side. How numerous are his children and servants!

glossa.text: *And there went crowds,* etc. The crowds that follow Jesus as he makes his way to Jerusalem signify those who, invited or compelled, come to the supper, and with their whole intent imitate Jesus going before them to the vision of eternal peace. These therefore he instructs, who ought with sincere love to seek that country, and for its sake to renounce the affections of carnal love.

*If any man come.* We can at once both hate and love: so that we love both those joined to us by acquaintance and by the divine precept, and those whom we suffer as adversaries in the way of God we may not know, by hating and fleeing them. *Yea more.* Then do we rightly hate our own soul, when we do not consent to its carnal desires, but struggle against them and break them.

*And whosoever doth not carry.* The cross is carried in two ways: either when the flesh is afflicted by abstinence, or when the mind is afflicted by compassion for a neighbour. *And come after me.* For if a man tears his flesh for empty glory, or has compassion on his neighbour carnally so as to favour his fault, he seems to bear the cross, but he does not follow God.

*For which of you.* After the Lord had given to those following him into Jerusalem lofty precepts concerning contempt of the world and the casting away of the body, he adds a precept concerning perseverance, for which patience with humility is necessary. And this by the likeness of one that builds. *To build a tower.* Because he had given lofty precepts, he subjoins a comparison of a loftiness to be built. *Reckoneth the charges.* He reckons the charges who discerns that temporal money must be paid out, and the heart turned away from the covetous desires of the world, and the soul made ready against the adversities of the world.

*All that see.* As the Apostle says: *We are made a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men ((II Cor. IV))*. And in everything that we do we ought to consider our hidden adversaries, who lie in wait for our works; and unless we watch against them, we suffer as mockers those whom we have as persuaders to evil.

*Or what,* etc. After the similitude of the tower to be built, he adds the similitude of a greater matter, of a king about to fight. In which it is shown that by the fulfilment of the preceding commandments no man can attain to glory unless the sentence of the severe judge be tempered by mercy. For in the sight of God every man is imperfect. *If he be able.* He meets God as it were with ten thousand who offers the works of the ten commandments which he has performed outwardly. But God comes against him as it were with a doubled number, when he examines him, scarcely prepared in work alone, at once concerning both work and thought. And therefore, while he is still far off through the delay of the judgment, we, considering the insufficiency of our frailty, ought to send before us, for the obtaining of the severe judge's peace, an embassy of tears, of good works, of holy affection.

*So likewise,* etc. He infers this from the foregoing similitudes. Since he cannot build well who does not reckon the charges, nor can he safely go to meet another who does not send an embassy before him, therefore neither can he be my disciple who does not renounce all things.

echoes.text: As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to those who send him; for he refreshes the soul of his masters.
echoes.note: Paul says the hearts (literally bowels/inward parts) of the saints have been 'refreshed' through Philemon. Proverbs likens a faithful messenger to the cold of snow that 'refreshes the soul' of his masters, the nearest sapiential parallel to this language of inward refreshment. The link is verbal and thematic rather than a citation, and Paul develops it more pointedly at v20.

echoes.text: “‘If your brother has grown poor among you, and sells himself to you; you shall not make him to serve as a slave. As a hired servant, and as a temporary resident, he shall be with you; he shall serve with you until the Year of Jubilee: then he shall go out from you, he and his children with him, and shall return to his own family, and to the possession of his fathers. For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. They shall not be […]
echoes.note: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus 'no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother.' The Holiness Code forbids treating an impoverished Israelite who sells himself as a slave, requiring instead that he be held as a hired worker and a brother, not ruled over harshly. Paul effectively extends this Israelite kinship-over-bondage principle to a Christian master and his returning slave.

echoes.text: If your brother, a Hebrew man, or a Hebrew woman, is sold to you, and serves you six years; then in the seventh year you shall let him go free from you. When you let him go free from you, you shall not let him go empty. You shall furnish him liberally out of your flock, out of your threshing floor, and out of your wine press. As Yahweh your God has blessed you, you shall give to him. You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and […]
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic slave law mandates release of a Hebrew bondservant and generous provision out of remembered solidarity ('you were a slave in Egypt'). Paul's reconfiguring of Onesimus from slave to beloved brother, no longer held under necessity, resonates with this manumission-and-fraternity ethic, though Paul never cites the statute.

echoes.text: You shall not deliver to his master a servant who has escaped from his master to you. He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place which he shall choose within one of your gates, where it pleases him best. You shall not oppress him.
echoes.note: The law forbids returning an escaped slave to his master and requires letting him dwell freely where he chooses. Paul's careful handling of the fugitive Onesimus, sending him back only as a free brother and asking Philemon not to reclaim him as property, stands in deliberate tension and dialogue with this provision. Many read the whole letter as Paul navigating around the spirit of this command.

echoes.text: Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life. For these two years the famine has been in the land, and there are yet five years, in which there will be neither plowing nor harvest. God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant in the earth, and to save you alive by a great deliverance. So now it wasn’t you who sent me here, but God, and he has made me a father to Pharaoh, lord […]
echoes.note: 'Perhaps he was separated from you for a while, that you would have him forever' echoes Joseph's providential reading of his own separation from his family: 'God sent me before you to preserve life... it was not you who sent me here, but God.' Paul, like Joseph, reframes a painful parting as hidden divine purpose that yields a greater, lasting reunion.

echoes.text: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save many people alive.
echoes.note: Joseph's summary, 'you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good,' undergirds Paul's 'perhaps' of v15, where Onesimus's wrong and flight are recast as occasion for good. The thematic kinship is strong even though Paul borrows no wording.

echoes.text: Laban said to him, “Surely you are my bone and my flesh.” He lived with him for a month.
echoes.note: Onesimus is now to be received as a brother 'both in the flesh and in the Lord.' Laban's welcome of Jacob, 'surely you are my bone and my flesh,' is the paradigmatic Hebrew idiom for kinship recognition that overrides prior status. The connection is faint and conceptual.

echoes.text: I’ll be collateral for him. From my hand will you require him. If I don’t bring him to you, and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever,
echoes.note: 'If he has wronged you or owes you anything, put that to my account... I will repay it' enacts the role of surety. Judah pledges himself for Benjamin: 'I will be surety for him; of my hand you shall require him.' Paul stands as personal guarantor for Onesimus exactly as Judah does for his brother, assuming the debt against himself.

echoes.text: For your servant became collateral for the boy to my father, saying, ‘If I don’t bring him to you, then I will bear the blame to my father forever.’
echoes.note: Judah restates his suretyship before Joseph, 'I became surety for the boy to my father,' offering to bear the consequence in the brother's place. Paul's handwritten pledge to absorb Onesimus's debt and stand in his stead closely parallels this self-substituting guarantee for a kinsman.

echoes.text: My son, if you have become collateral for your neighbor, if you have struck your hands in pledge for a stranger; You are trapped by the words of your mouth. You are ensnared with the words of your mouth. Do this now, my son, and deliver yourself, since you have come into the hand of your neighbor. Go, humble yourself. Press your plea with your neighbor.
echoes.note: Proverbs repeatedly treats the giving of surety for another as a weighty, self-binding act ('if you have struck your hands in pledge for a stranger... you are snared by the words of your mouth'). Paul knowingly takes on precisely this binding pledge for Onesimus, inverting the proverb's caution into voluntary love.

echoes.text: He who is collateral for a stranger will suffer for it, but he who refuses pledges of collateral is secure.
echoes.note: 'He who is surety for a stranger will suffer for it.' Paul's assumption of Onesimus's liability deliberately embraces the cost the proverb warns against, making the sapiential surety-language a backdrop for his act of intercession.

echoes.text: As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to those who send him; for he refreshes the soul of his masters.
echoes.note: 'Refresh my heart in the Lord' picks up the language of inward refreshment from v7. Proverbs' image of the faithful messenger who 'refreshes the soul of his masters' is the closest wisdom parallel to this petition for refreshment as the fruit of obedient love.

echoes.text: It fell on a day, that Elisha passed to Shunem, where there was a prominent woman; and she persuaded him to eat bread. So it was, that as often as he passed by, he turned in there to eat bread. She said to her husband, “See now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God, that passes by us continually. Please let us make a little room on the wall. Let us set for him there a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp stand. It shall be, when he comes to us, that he […]
echoes.note: 'Prepare a guest room for me' faintly recalls the Shunammite woman who prepares a small upper room for Elisha so the man of God may lodge with her. The shared motif is hospitality of a lodging readied for an honored servant of God, though Paul uses ordinary travel language without scriptural signal.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.
echoes.note: 'If anyone... doesn't disregard his own father, mother, wife, children' echoes the blessing of Levi, who said of father and mother 'I have not seen him,' disowned his brothers and ignored his children — keeping covenant fidelity above kin. The radical preference of covenant loyalty over family ties is the closest scriptural precedent for Jesus' hyperbolic 'hate.'

echoes.text: He said to them, “Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, ‘Every man put his sword on his thigh, and go back and forth from gate to gate throughout the camp, and every man kill his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbor.’” The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses: and there fell of the people that day about three thousand men. Moses said, “Consecrate yourselves today to Yahweh, yes, every man against his son, and against […]
echoes.note: The Levites' ordination by slaying brother, companion, and neighbor at Moses' command — 'each one at the cost of his son and his brother' — is the narrative behind Deut 33:9's praise of Levi. It models the disciple's willingness to set covenant allegiance above family, coherent with Jesus' demand and the cross-bearing that follows.

echoes.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
echoes.note: Micah's portrait of eschatological family division — son dishonoring father, daughter against mother, 'a man's enemies are the men of his own household' — undergirds Jesus' setting discipleship against the closest kin (and is explicitly cited at Luke 12:53). Recurrence in Luke strengthens its availability here.

echoes.text: If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son, or your daughter, or the wife of your bosom, or your friend, who is as your own soul, entices you secretly, saying, “Let us go and serve other gods,” which you have not known, you, nor your fathers; of the gods of the peoples who are around you, near to you, or far off from you, from the one end of the earth even to the other end of the earth; you shall not consent to him, nor listen to him; neither […]
echoes.note: The command to show no pity even to a brother, son, daughter, or wife who entices to false worship — placing exclusive devotion to the Lord above the dearest relations — offers a Torah analogue to subordinating family to higher allegiance. Faint and contested, but coheres with the covenant-over-kin theme of Deut 33:9.

echoes.text: for by wise guidance you wage your war; and victory is in many advisors.
echoes.note: The king who 'will not sit down first and consider' before going to war reflects the proverb 'by wise guidance you can wage your war, and in an abundance of counselors there is victory.' The counsel to deliberate before battle is the sapiential ground of Jesus' second illustration about counting the cost.

echoes.text: Plans are established by advice; by wise guidance you wage war!
echoes.note: 'Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war' doubles the counting-the-cost-before-war motif of vv.31-32. Recurrence of this maxim across Proverbs 20:18 and 24:6 strengthens the wisdom-deliberation background of the tower-and-war pair.

echoes.text: Prepare your work outside, and get your fields ready. Afterwards, build your house.
echoes.note: 'Prepare your work outside... and after that build your house' supplies the prudence-before-building logic behind the tower illustration ('count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it'). Faint but coherent with the sapiential planning theme.

echoes.text: Let reason be the beginning of every work, And let counsel go before every action.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's 'before every action let counsel go, and before every undertaking deliberation' captures the count-the-cost-first principle of both illustrations. Deuterocanonical availability adds Second-Temple recurrence to the wisdom-deliberation reading.

registers.label: Spare
lines: O Lord, you have searched us and known us.
You knit us together, and our days were written before one came to be.
Like clay on the wheel, we are in the potter's hands.
Shape us, mend us, make us new.
Jesus turns and says, count the cost, take up your cross, and follow.
We come holding nothing back.
Come, you who are wonderfully made, and worship.
We are the clay; you are the potter. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Jeremiah went down to the potter's house and watched the wheel spin, the wet clay rising under two steady hands, collapsing, and rising again.
We are the clay; you are the potter.
When the vessel was spoiled, the potter did not throw it out — he gathered it up and worked it into another shape, good in his eyes.
We are the clay; you are the potter.
This is the God who searched you and knew you, who formed your inward parts and held you before your first breath.
We are the clay; you are the potter.
So bring the marred places, the parts you would hide, and set them on the wheel. Count the cost, follow, and let the Maker make you new.
We are the clay; you are the potter. Amen.

lines: You searched us, knew us, formed us in the dark.
